summary: Describes the Congestion Manager, an end-system module that lets several concurrent streams from a sender to the same receiver share congestion information. Together they perform congestion avoidance and control, and applications can adapt more easily to network congestion.

plainLanguage.summary: When many kids share one narrow hallway, a hall monitor tells them how fast to go so they don't jam up together.

subtitle: An end-host module that lets all streams to the same receiver share one view of network congestion.

tldr.problem: Concurrent streams to the same receiver compete instead of sharing, and together they tend to be more aggressive in congestion than one TCP connection. Many real-time UDP applications do not react to congestion at all.
tldr.mechanism: The Congestion Manager keeps congestion state per macroflow, and applications use an API to ask permission to send, report what happened, and learn the current rate and round-trip time. A congestion controller decides when data may go and a scheduler decides which stream goes.
tldr.outcome: Streams share congestion information and applications can adapt what they send. It is a Proposed Standard whose use is optional, and the document leaves feedback for applications without their own feedback, and differentiated-service networks, to later documents.

facts.label: Grant size
facts.value: Up to one PMTU of bytes per cm_request()

today: RFC 3124 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says systems MAY choose to use the CM, and that extensions for applications without their own feedback and for differentiated-service networks would come in later documents.

sections.title: Why a Congestion Manager
sections.content:
The Congestion Manager (CM) is an end-system module with two goals. The first is efficient multiplexing. Servers send many kinds of data to a receiver, and the streams share a path but usually compete for it and do not learn from each other. Even if each stream does its own congestion control, the group tends to be more aggressive in congestion than a single TCP connection.

The second goal is application adaptation. Popular real-time streaming applications run over UDP with their own user-level transports and in most cases do not react properly to congestion. By implementing a stable control algorithm and exposing an adaptation API, the CM lets applications adapt what they transmit to current conditions.

The design builds on TCP control block sharing and integrated TCP congestion control, and extends them to non-TCP streams and to an API for adaptation. Systems MAY choose to use the CM, and if so they MUST follow this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Several kids all running down the same hallway shove each other. If they share information about how crowded it is, everybody gets through more smoothly.

sections.title: Scope and Key Terms
sections.content:
The document focuses on well-behaved applications that have their own per-byte or per-packet sequence numbers and use the CM API to update CM state, on best-effort networks without reservations. The receiving application must give feedback to the sender about received packets and losses, and no changes to the receiver protocol stack are required. It does not address networks with reservations or service differentiation, nor streams to the same host that cross paths with differing characteristics.

Key terms:

  • Stream: packets sharing source and destination IP address, type-of-service, transport protocol and ports.
  • Macroflow: a group of CM-enabled streams that use the same congestion management and scheduling algorithms and share congestion state. Streams to different receivers belong to different macroflows. Streams with identical congestion behavior and algorithm SHOULD share a macroflow.
  • Well-behaved application: one that only transmits when the CM allows and accurately reports what it sent.
  • cwnd and ownd: the congestion window, and the bytes sent but not known to be received or lost.
sections.plainLanguage: A stream is one conversation. A macroflow is all the conversations going to the same place, which share a single traffic report.

sections.title: Components of the Framework
sections.content:
The framework has three key components: the API, the congestion controller and the scheduler. The congestion controller adjusts the aggregate transmission rate between sender and receiver from its estimate of congestion, using feedback that applications give through the API. The scheduler divides available bandwidth among the streams of a macroflow and tells applications when they may send.

The CM does not enforce proper behavior for all applications, though it does not preclude a policer on the host. The network itself must still be protected against compromised end hosts, which needs router machinery and is not addressed.

Each macroflow has its own congestion control algorithm, which MUST be "TCP-friendly". The controller MUST implement abstract query, notify and update interfaces so that separately developed schedulers can interoperate, and MUST call the scheduler's schedule function when the congestion state allows an MTU-sized packet to be sent. The scheduler MUST implement schedule, query_share and notify.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper decides how much traffic the road can take. Another decides whose turn it is to drive. Together they keep the road moving.

sections.title: The CM API
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the IETF does not by convention treat APIs as standards track, but wants API and algorithm requirements in one document. The functions are abstract and implementations may differ in detail.

State: applications MUST call cm_open(stream_info) first, which returns a cm_streamid (or -1 on failure), and SHOULD call cm_close at the end. cm_mtu returns the estimated path MTU.

Sending comes in two styles. In the callback style the application calls cm_request and the CM later calls cmapp_send(), a grant to send up to one PMTU of bytes. The CM buffers no data, so the stream can adapt at the last instant. In the synchronous style, used by timer-driven senders, the CM calls cmapp_update(newrate, srtt, rttdev) when the rate changes and the stream MUST keep within it. cm_thresh sets how large a change must be before callbacks, and cm_query reads the current rate and round-trip estimates, returning negative values when no valid estimate exists.

Feedback: when a stream hears from the receiver it MUST call cm_update with bytes received, bytes lost, a loss mode and an RTT sample. cm_notify MUST be called when data is actually sent. A cmapp_send grant expires after the larger of the round-trip time and an implementation-dependent threshold, and an application that declines to send SHOULD call cm_notify with 0 so other streams can use the grant. The CM MUST be robust to applications that forget or crash.

Grouping: cm_getmacroflow and cm_setmacroflow let applications choose which streams share a macroflow. The suggested default is to aggregate by destination IP address. The RFC warns that hosts behind a NAT look like one address, so those on different bottleneck links may see worse performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, a program asks the CM, 'may I?'. After sending, it tells the CM what happened. The CM can also say, 'the road got slower, please send less.'

sections.title: Loss Reporting and Feedback
sections.content:
The lossmode argument of cm_update tells the CM how a loss was found, and is reported as a bit-vector:

  • CM_NO_FEEDBACK: no feedback for all outstanding data, such as a TCP timeout.
  • CM_LOSS_FEEDBACK: some loss believed due to congestion, but not all outstanding data lost, such as loss found through duplicate acknowledgments.
  • CM_EXPLICIT_CONGESTION: the receiver echoed an explicit congestion notification.
  • CM_NO_CONGESTION: no congestion-related loss. On links with non-congestion losses an application SHOULD still report them with this flag set.

All applications that use the CM MUST incorporate receiver feedback, typically once or twice per round-trip time, and MUST call cm_update with the result. This updates ownd and may change estimates and trigger cmapp_update callbacks.
sections.plainLanguage: After each delivery the program tells the CM whether the packages arrived, were lost, or the road signs said 'slow down'. The CM uses these reports to judge traffic.

sections.title: Examples: TCP, UDP and Audio
sections.content:
The RFC gives three example uses and says they are suggestions, not requirements.

TCP over the CM uses the cmapp_send callback. TCP removes its own congestion window checks and slow-start threshold updates, still does loss recovery, queues data and calls cm_request, and sends at most one segment per callback. On three duplicate acknowledgments it reports a loss with CM_LOSS_FEEDBACK, and on a retransmission timeout it reports CM_NO_FEEDBACK.

Congestion-controlled UDP buffers data in a socket queue, calls cm_request, and sends one MTU per callback. It needs feedback either from the receiving application or from the receiving UDP implementation, and the latter needs changes to the receiver's stack and explicit negotiation.

An audio server uses the synchronous API: it queries the CM at start, picks an encoding that fits the estimate (or its own initial values if the estimate is negative) and changes encoding when cmapp_update reports a new rate.

The RFC also sketches an additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease controller (AIMD_CC) and a round robin scheduler (RR_sched), whose query_share returns 1/(number of streams in macroflow).
sections.plainLanguage: The same traffic helper works for different kinds of travelers: a file download, a live call, a music stream. Each learns how much road is free and fits itself in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the CM offers much of what TCP congestion control offers, it shares many of the same weaknesses. Wrong reports of losses and transmissions give it an inaccurate picture of congestion. A high estimate of congestion degrades performance, and a stream on a host can arbitrarily slow down any other stream on the same macroflow, a form of denial of service.

The more dangerous case is a low estimate of congestion, which makes the CM overly aggressive and lets data go out much faster than sound congestion control would allow.

Applications can also control shared state through the API that affects other applications on the same computer. For example, a poorly designed, compromised or malicious UDP application could misuse cm_update to starve others in the macroflow or make them too aggressive.
sections.plainLanguage: If one kid tells the hall monitor false things, the whole hallway suffers: everyone slows down, or everyone runs too fast and crashes.

viz.caption: THE THREE KEY COMPONENTS OF THE CM FRAMEWORK

items.title: API
items.text: Lets applications open streams, request transmissions, report feedback and query rate and round-trip time.

items.title: Congestion controller
items.text: Decides when and how much a macroflow may send, from feedback reported by applications.

items.title: Scheduler
items.text: Decides which stream of the macroflow gets to transmit and notifies applications when they may send.

messages.label: cm_request()
messages.note: Asks for a chance to send up to one PMTU of bytes.

messages.label: cmapp_send()
messages.note: Grant to send, valid until it expires.

messages.label: cm_notify(nsent)
messages.note: Reports that data was actually sent.

messages.label: feedback
messages.note: The receiving application reports received packets and losses.

messages.label: cm_update(nrecd, nlost, lossmode, rtt)
messages.note: Passes the feedback on to the CM.

items.label: No feedback
items.desc: No feedback for any outstanding data, such as a TCP timeout.

items.label: Loss
items.desc: Some loss thought to be congestion, but not all outstanding data lost.

items.label: Explicit congestion
items.desc: The receiver echoed an explicit congestion notification.
